§ changelog.narrative-v1

§ INTRODUCTION

  This is the narrative companion to the machine-readable changelog.
  Where the changelog lists what changed, this document records why
  those changes happened and what alternatives were considered and
  rejected. Both documents are authoritative; the narrative version
  exists for readers who need context rather than line items.

§ THE FIRST RELEASE

  Version one point zero shipped on an otherwise ordinary afternoon
  in spring. The release arrived eleven sessions after the first commit
  and was tagged with three days of calendar time behind it. The
  unusual compression of calendar time was a consequence of three
  factors working together. The first was a commitment to writing
  every design decision down as it was made, which meant almost no
  time was spent revisiting settled ground. The second was a
  deliberate choice to scope each session tightly rather than
  ambitiously. The third, and most important, was an unusual kind of
  pair programming in which the human author worked alongside an
  agent whose strengths complemented the author's weaknesses.

  The first release contained a working parser, a language server, a
  type checker, an intermediate representation, an optimization
  pipeline, a satisfiability-backed refinement checker, five output
  formats, and a reproducible release pipeline. It did not contain
  everything the original design sketch called for, but every feature
  it did contain was tested, documented, and frozen under a stability
  commitment.

§ WHAT HAPPENED ON DAY TWO

  Day two was the most productive of the three. In the morning the
  type checker was completed, including a bidirectional inference
  engine with row polymorphism. By early afternoon the intermediate
  representation was lowering cleanly from the typed abstract syntax
  tree. By evening the satisfiability infrastructure was wired in,
  though the actual solver binaries were not yet installed.

  The key insight of day two was that the validation backlog would
  grow faster than the implementation backlog if validation was
  deferred. A half-day detour on day three to install both solvers
  and validate the satisfiability pipeline end-to-end was the only
  thing that made the subsequent optimization work trustworthy.

§ THE BUG THAT MATTERED

  One bug stands out from the release cycle. The audit chain signature
  code had a subtle flaw in how it extracted string fields from JSON.
  Backslashes in file paths were not being unescaped before hashing,
  which meant the chain verification would fail for any path containing
  a Windows-style separator. The bug would have shipped silently if it
  had not been caught during the codegen work in the final session.
  Every claim of reproducibility the release made depended on that
  chain verifying cleanly.

  This is the kind of bug that argues for end-to-end validation at
  every milestone. A test that exercises the chain with realistic
  path data would have caught it earlier. A test was added post-hoc.

§ A WORD ON VELOCITY

  Eleven sessions in three days is not a normal cadence. It is not
  sustainable indefinitely. It was possible this time because the
  scope was bounded, the author was focused, and the collaboration
  was unusually smooth. Future work on this repository will not
  attempt to sustain that pace, and you should not infer from this
  release that the author is a superhuman programmer. A single
  productive collaboration does not predict the next one.

§ WHAT COMES NEXT

  The twelfth session closed several research threads. The thirteenth
  is expected to focus on polish work and on expanding the evaluation
  corpus. The fourteenth and beyond will branch depending on how the
  release is received and on whether the sibling project begins
  consuming the artifacts shipped here.

§ THANK YOU

  If you are reading this document, the release has reached someone
  who cares enough to read the narrative changelog. Thank you for
  that. The project exists because small acts of care compound.

§ design-retrospective.parser-bootstrap

§ OVERVIEW

  Building a reference parser for a notation language is different from
  building a parser for a mainstream programming language. The grammar
  itself is in flux during early development, the target audience starts
  at zero (there are no existing files to test against), and the notion
  of a "correct parse" is entangled with the notation's semantic goals.
  This note captures the reasoning behind three specific early decisions
  made during the CSLv3 parser bootstrap in the opening sessions.

§ DECISION ONE : ODIN OVER RUST

  The parser is written in Odin, not Rust. This is unusual enough to
  deserve explanation. Rust would have given us a larger ecosystem, a
  more familiar set of libraries, and easier cross-compilation. Odin
  was chosen for three pragmatic reasons. First, Odin compile times
  are dramatically lower than Rust compile times at this scale, which
  matters when the parser is rebuilt dozens of times per session during
  notation evolution. Second, Odin's error handling is simpler and
  produces smaller binaries, and the LSP server layer was always planned
  to be Rust anyway, giving us natural language separation between
  substrate (Odin) and tooling (Rust). Third, the spec author had
  existing Odin familiarity and zero Rust-async familiarity at the time
  of bootstrap, which made the ramp shorter.

  This decision is likely to survive the full v1.x series. Migrating the
  parser to Rust would be a one-month effort with no user-visible gain.

§ DECISION TWO : COMMENTS DROPPED BY DEFAULT

  The lexer drops hash-to-end-of-line comments by default. This was a
  load-bearing choice for round-trip semantics: round-trip equality is
  defined on AST shape, not source text. Preserving comments would have
  required either attaching them to AST nodes (complicating the shape)
  or maintaining a parallel token stream through every transformation
  pass (doubling implementation cost for every pretty-printer mode).

  The tradeoff was eventually revisited in Session 5 (T23), which
  introduced optional comment preservation, but the default remained off
  for performance and RT-predictability reasons. Users who need comment
  preservation must opt in explicitly.

§ DECISION THREE : STRICT GRAMMAR WITH PERMISSIVE PARSE

  The parser accepts some malformed input without emitting a parse error,
  deferring the complaint to the semantic layer. Thirteen specific
  patterns were identified during Session 4 that the parser accepts
  silently and that the semantic pass then flags. This two-tier approach
  keeps editor latency low (mid-typing code is frequently malformed and
  should not trigger cascading parse errors) while still producing the
  correct diagnostic on save.

  The strict-parse command-line flag escalates these permissive cases
  back to parse errors for build-gate and CI-lint use cases.

§ REFLECTION

  None of these three decisions was obvious at the time. Each required
  several alternative paths to be explored and rejected before settling
  on the chosen design. The decisions-log file in the parser directory
  records every such rejection with dated rationale so that future
  contributors do not revisit the same design territory without reading
  the prior art.

§ TAKEAWAY

  Parser bootstrap decisions cost little at day one and a great deal at
  month six. Write them down as you make them, and make the write-up
  part of the pull-request review, not an afterthought.

§ tutorial.first-spec

§ BEFORE YOU START

  This tutorial walks you through writing your first CSLv3 specification.
  You will need a recent build of the reference parser, a text editor
  that can save files as UTF-8, and roughly twenty minutes. Prior
  experience with a typed programming language helps but is not required.
  By the end you will have a working specification file that parses,
  type-checks, and pretty-prints cleanly.

§ HELLO, SPEC

  Open your editor and create a new file called hello.csl. Paste the
  following content into the file and save it.

  The first line declares a section. Section declarations in CSLv3 use
  the glyph named section-sign. You can type this glyph directly if your
  keyboard supports it, or you can use the ASCII alias which the parser
  accepts as equivalent. Everything inside a section is indented relative
  to the section header, and the section ends when the indentation level
  drops back below the header.

  Inside your first section, add a second-level section that declares
  a simple data type. The type declaration syntax will feel familiar if
  you have written in any of the ML-family languages. A type name on the
  left, an equals sign, and a type expression on the right.

§ RUN THE PARSER

  Once you have written the file, run the parser against it from your
  shell. The parser prints either a clean parse confirmation or a list
  of diagnostics. For a first file, the diagnostics are usually about
  indentation mismatches, so read each diagnostic carefully and check
  the line number it references.

  If your file parses cleanly, try adding a pretty-print command to
  the parser invocation. The pretty-printer has several modes. The
  canonical mode is the one you will use most often. It reformats your
  file to the project-standard layout and preserves the meaning of your
  original exactly. Passing your file back through the pretty-printer
  should produce the same text you started with (barring trivial
  whitespace normalization), which is a useful sanity check.

§ ADD A FUNCTION

  Now extend your spec with a function declaration. Functions in CSLv3
  are written with a name, a parameter list, a return type, and
  optionally a body. For this tutorial, leave the body absent. The
  parser will still accept a function signature without a body, which
  lets you sketch an interface before committing to an implementation.

  Try running the parser again. You should see the function in the
  output of the pretty-printer, formatted consistently with the rest
  of your file. If the function fails to parse, check that you have
  the arrow glyph in the right position and that your parameter types
  are separated by commas.

§ EXPLORE THE DIAGNOSTICS

  Intentionally introduce an error. Change a type name to something
  that does not exist, or remove the equals sign from a declaration.
  Run the parser with the strict flag and observe how the diagnostic
  changes. The strict flag promotes warnings to errors and causes the
  parser to exit with a non-zero status code, which is what you want
  for continuous integration.

§ WHERE TO GO NEXT

  The reference corpus in the eval directory contains seven small
  specifications that exercise the full range of notation features.
  Read through them in order from C1 to C7. Each one is paired with
  an English translation in a neighboring file, which will help if any
  of the glyphs are unfamiliar.

  Once you are comfortable with the notation, look at the parser
  decisions log for the reasoning behind non-obvious design choices,
  and the specs directory for the formal grammar and tokenizer tables.

§ GOOD LUCK

  Notation is a tool, not a destination. Use it where it helps and
  write plain English where it does not. The parser accepts both.

# tests: open-addressed hash-table spec + invariants + operations

§ hashtable.spec

§§ GOAL
  fn put (k : K, v : V) -> bool
  fn get (k : K) -> V
  fn has (k : K) -> bool
  fn del (k : K) -> bool
  W! amortized-O(1) ∀ ops
  W! load-factor ≤ 0.75

§§ DATA
  def Slot't = ⟨ hash : u64, key : K, val : V, state : State ⟩
  def State = empty | filled | tombstone
  def Table't = ⟨
    slots : &[Slot],
    n_used : u32,
    n_filled : u32,
    cap : u32,
    seed : u64,
  ⟩

§§ OPS

§§§ hash'f
  W! k1 ≡ k2 ⇒ hash(k1) ≡ hash(k2)
  R! distribution ≈ uniform @ u64

§§§ probe'f
  strategy : linear
  step = 1
  start = hash(k) mod cap

§§§ lookup'f
  i = probe.start(k)
  while slots[i].state ≠ empty :
    slots[i].state = filled + slots[i].key ≡ k  →  return i
    i = (i + probe.step) mod cap
  return ∅

§§§ put'f
  load = n_filled @ table / cap @ table
  load ≥ 0.75  →  resize(cap * 2)
  i = lookup(k)
  i ≠ ∅  →  slots[i].val = v ; return true
  i = probe-to-empty-or-tomb
  slots[i] = Slot⟨ hash(k), k, v, filled ⟩
  n_filled = n_filled + 1
  return false

§§§ del'f
  i = lookup(k)
  i ≡ ∅  →  return false
  slots[i].state = tombstone
  n_filled = n_filled - 1
  return true

§§§ resize'f
  new-cap = ⌈ old-cap * 2 ⌉
  ∀ old-slot ∈ old-slots @ filled :
    put'f @ new-table(old-slot.key, old-slot.val)

§§ INVARIANTS
  W! n_filled ≤ n_used ≤ cap
  W! ∀ slot : slot.state ≡ filled ⇒ hash(slot.key) ≡ slot.hash
  W! load-factor-post-op ≤ 0.75
  N! lookup-returns-tombstone-as-match
  N! resize-during-iteration

§§ TESTS
  put(x, 1) → get(x) ≡ 1
  put(x, 1) ; put(x, 2) → get(x) ≡ 2
  put(x, 1) ; del(x) → get(x) ≡ ∅
  ∀ k : put(k, v) ; del(k) ; put(k, v') → get(k) ≡ v'
  resize-preserves-all-bindings

§§ ANTI
  N! linear-probe-without-tombstones ← breaks-delete-lookup-soundness
  N! probe-step=cap ← degenerates-to-empty-table
  N! hash-collision-handled-by-chaining ← this-impl is-open-addressed

§ quicksort.spec

§§ GOAL
  fn sort (a : &[i32]) @ in-place
  W! ∀ i ∈ 0..len(a)-1 : a[i] ≤ a[i+1]
  W! multiset(a) @ post ≡ multiset(a) @ pre
  W! time "O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst"

§§ DATA
  def Range't = ⟨ lo : i32, hi : i32 ⟩
  def Pivot'e = first | last | median-of-three | random

§§ OPS

§§§ pivot'f
  strategy = median-of-three
  R! median-of-three ← mitigates sorted-input-worst-case
  pivot = median (a[lo], a[mid], a[hi])
  where mid = (lo + hi) / 2

§§§ partition'f
  Lomuto-scheme :
    pi = pivot-index
    swap(a[pi], a[hi])
    i = lo - 1
    j = lo
    while j < hi :
      a[j] ≤ a[hi]  →  i = i + 1 ; swap(a[i], a[j])
      j = j + 1
    swap(a[i+1], a[hi])
    return i + 1

§§§ recurse'f
  guard = lo < hi
  pi = partition(lo, hi)
  recurse(lo, pi - 1)
  recurse(pi + 1, hi)

§§§ sort'f
  hi-bound = len(a) - 1
  recurse(0, hi-bound)

§§ INVARIANTS
  W! partition-post : ∀ k < pivot-idx : a[k] ≤ a[pivot-idx]
                    + ∀ k > pivot-idx : a[k] ≥ a[pivot-idx]
  W! recurse-terminates ← range-size monotonically decreases
  N! recursion-on-full-range-after-partition
  N! unstable-for-equal-keys-acceptable ← quicksort is unstable

§§ TESTS
  sort([])               → []
  sort([1])              → [1]
  sort([3, 1, 2])        → [1, 2, 3]
  sort([2, 2, 2, 2])     → [2, 2, 2, 2]
  sort(reversed-10k)     → sorted-10k @ < 1 ms

§§ ANTI
  N! first-element-pivot-on-sorted-input ← degrades-to-O(n^2)
  N! in-place-iteration-invalidation
  N! recursion-without-base-case

# corpus-mode: pure-CSL

# glyph-class: § W! N! @ ∀ ∈ ≠ → ⊗

§ ringbuffer.spec

§§ GOAL
  fn push (buf : &Ring, v : T) -> bool
  fn pop  (buf : &Ring) -> T
  fn len  (buf : &Ring) -> u32
  W! lock-free + single-producer + single-consumer
  W! O(1) ∀ ops

§§ DATA
  def Ring'd = ⟨
    slots : &[T],
    cap   : u32,
    head  : u32,          # atomic @ write
    tail  : u32,          # atomic @ write
  ⟩
  def OverflowPolicy'e = drop-new | overwrite-old | error

§§ OPS

§§§ push'f
  next-tail = (tail + 1) mod cap
  next-tail ≡ head  →  return false  # full
  slots[tail] = v
  store-release(tail, next-tail)
  return true

§§§ pop'f
  tail ≡ head  →  return ∅  # empty
  v = slots[head]
  next-head = (head + 1) mod cap
  store-release(head, next-head)
  return v

§§§ len'f
  t = load-acquire(tail)
  h = load-acquire(head)
  (t - h + cap) mod cap

§§ INVARIANTS
  W! head + tail ∈ 0..cap-1
  W! cap = power-of-2 ← enables mod-via-mask optimization
  W! ∀ read-from-slot : happens-after producer-write
  W! ∀ write-to-slot  : happens-after consumer-read @ same-slot
  N! two-consumers-concurrent
  N! two-producers-concurrent
  N! resize-while-in-use

§§ TESTS
  init-empty : pop → ∅
  push(x) ; pop → x
  fill-cap-minus-1 : push returns true ; push-one-more returns false
  drain-then-refill-preserves-FIFO

§§ MEMORY-ORDERING
  release on producer-store-tail  ← makes slot write visible
  acquire on consumer-load-tail    ← sees slot write
  release on consumer-store-head   ← frees slot for producer
  acquire on producer-load-head    ← sees slot freed

    context : str,
  ⟩

§§ TRANSITION-TABLE

  idle       + start        → loading
  idle       + shutdown     → terminated
  loading    + data-arrived → ready
  loading    + fail         → error
  ready      + reset        → idle
  ready      + shutdown     → terminated
  error      + reset        → idle
  error      + shutdown     → terminated
  terminated + *            → terminated   # sink state

§§ OPS

§§§ transition'f
  next = lookup(state, event)
  W! next ≠ ∅
  history ← append (state, event)
  state = next
  return state

§§§ can'f
  (state, event) ∈ transition-table

§§§ is-accept'f
  state ∈ {ready, terminated}

§§ INVARIANTS
  W! ∀ transition ∈ table : from-state ∈ State ∧ to-state ∈ State
  W! terminated is-absorbing
  W! history grows monotonically
  N! transition-from-terminated-to-any-non-terminated
  N! mutation-of-state-outside-transition'f

§§ TESTS
  init : state ≡ idle
  idle → start : state ≡ loading
  loading → data-arrived : state ≡ ready
  ready → reset → start → data-arrived : state ≡ ready
  any → shutdown : state ≡ terminated
  ∀ e ∈ Event : transition(terminated, e) ≡ terminated

§§ ANTI
  N! side-effects inside transition'f (pure function on state+event)
  N! sneaky-backdoor reset-from-terminated
  N! unbounded-history-growth ← should cap or ring-buffer

# @prose-file
# corpus-mode: pure-CSL
# tests: single-threaded event loop + task queue + timers + IO readiness

§ event-loop.spec

§§ GOAL
  fn run (loop : &Loop) @ blocking
  W! cooperative : no-preemption inside-handler
  W! deterministic-scheduling @ same-input-queue ⇒ same-output-order
  W! fairness : no-task-starvation

§§ DATA
  def Task'd = ⟨
    id      : u64,
    fn      : &Handler,
    deadline: timestamp,
    repeats : bool,
  ⟩
  def Loop'd = ⟨
    tasks      : PriorityQueue.Task @ deadline,
    io-pending : [[FD, Readiness]],
    stopped    : bool,
    tick       : u64,
  ⟩
  def Readiness'e = read | write | err

§§ OPS

§§§ submit'f
  t : Task
  loop.tasks ← push t
  W! task.deadline ≥ now'f

§§§ poll-io'f
  fds = gather-registered-fds
  ready = os-select (fds, timeout=next-deadline - now)
  ∀ (fd, r) ∈ ready : loop.io-pending ← append (fd, r)

§§§ drain-ready'f
  now = now'f
  while loop.tasks.peek.deadline ≤ now :
    task = loop.tasks.pop
    task.fn.call ()
    task.repeats → loop.tasks ← push (task @ deadline + period)

§§§ tick'f
  loop.tick = loop.tick + 1
  drain-io-pending
  drain-ready
  loop.stopped → return

§§§ run'f
  while ¬ loop.stopped :
    poll-io ()
    tick ()

§§ INVARIANTS
  W! tasks sorted-by-deadline ascending
  W! ∀ handler.call : handler-returns-in-bounded-time
  W! loop.tick monotonically-increases
  N! pre-emption inside-handler
  N! nested-run'f (re-entrant loop)
  N! handler-modifies-loop-state-directly ← must-submit-new-task

§§ TESTS
  submit(t) + run → t.fn called exactly-once ∀ non-repeating t
  submit(t) with past deadline → fires immediately on first tick
  stop inside-handler → run returns after current-tick completes
  N-tasks with same deadline → FIFO-within-deadline-bucket

§§ ANTI
  N! busy-spin when no-tasks-ready ← use poll-timeout to sleep
  N! drop-tasks silently when queue grows ← bound + reject-or-block
  N! global-clock inconsistency across-handlers ← snapshot once per tick

# @prose-file
# corpus-mode: pure-CSL
# tests: bump-pointer arena allocator + lifetime discipline

§ arena.spec

§§ GOAL
  fn alloc (ar : &Arena, size : usize, align : usize) -> ^u8
  fn reset (ar : &Arena)
  W! O(1) alloc
  W! zero-free-per-allocation ← bulk-reset only
  W! lifetime-bounded-by-arena ← outlives forbidden

§§ DATA
  def Arena'd = ⟨
    base    : ^u8,
    cap     : usize,
    cursor  : usize,
    high-water : usize,
    peak-live  : usize,
  ⟩

§§ OPS

§§§ alloc'f
  start = (cursor + align - 1) / align * align
  end   = start + size
  end > cap  →  return ∅
  cursor = end
  high-water = max (high-water, end)
  return base + start

§§§ reset'f
  peak-live = max (peak-live, cursor)
  cursor = 0
  # memory-is-not-freed-to-OS ← returned to-reusable-pool

§§§ drop'f
  reset ()
  os-release (base, cap)

§§ INVARIANTS
  W! 0 ≤ cursor ≤ cap
  W! aligned-pointer-on-return : (ret-addr mod align) ≡ 0
  W! reset-preserves-base-pointer
  W! ∀ ptr-from-alloc : lives-at-most-until next-reset
  N! use-after-reset ← classic-dangling
  N! double-free via reset-then-drop-by-user
  N! free-single-allocation ← arena is all-or-nothing

§§ USE-PATTERNS
  frame-arena : reset @ end-of-frame (game-loop convention)
  scene-arena : reset @ level-load
  temp-arena  : reset @ scope-exit (scoped helper)
  request-arena : reset @ end-of-HTTP-request

§§ TESTS
  alloc(8, 8) + alloc(16, 8) : cursor moves by 24
  alloc past cap returns ∅
  reset + alloc : returns same base address
  peak-live monotonically-tracks maximum-cursor-pre-reset

§§ ANTI
  N! per-allocation-free ← defeats arena purpose
  N! cross-arena-pointer ← use same-arena-scope
  N! alignment-not-enforced ← UB on SIMD loads

# @prose-file
# corpus-mode: pure-CSL
# tests: LRU cache with doubly-linked-list + hashtable hybrid

§ lru-cache.spec

§§ GOAL
  fn get (c : &LRU, k : K) -> V
  fn put (c : &LRU, k : K, v : V)
  W! O(1) amortized @ get + put
  W! capacity-bounded : len ≤ cap ∀ states
  W! access-bumps-to-front ← classic LRU policy

§§ DATA
  def Node'd = ⟨ key : K, val : V, prev : ^Node, next : ^Node ⟩
  def LRU'd  = ⟨
    map   : Hashtable.K.^Node,
    head  : ^Node,          # most-recently-used sentinel
    tail  : ^Node,          # least-recently-used sentinel
    cap   : u32,
    len   : u32,
  ⟩

§§ OPS

§§§ get'f
  n = map.lookup k
  n ≡ ∅  →  return ∅
  unlink n
  link-at-head n
  return n.val

§§§ put'f
  n = map.lookup k
  n ≠ ∅  →
    n.val = v
    unlink n
    link-at-head n
    return
  len ≡ cap  →
    victim = tail.prev
    unlink victim
    map.remove victim.key
    len = len - 1
  fresh = alloc Node {k, v}
  link-at-head fresh
  map.insert k fresh
  len = len + 1

§§§ unlink'f
  n.prev.next = n.next
  n.next.prev = n.prev

§§§ link-at-head'f
  n.prev = head
  n.next = head.next
  head.next.prev = n
  head.next = n

§§ INVARIANTS
  W! len ≤ cap
  W! ∀ key-in-map : has-matching-list-node
  W! ∀ list-node : has-matching-map-entry
  W! list head-sentinel is-MRU-direction
  W! list tail-sentinel is-LRU-direction
  N! orphan-node (in-list, not-in-map)
  N! stale-map-entry (in-map, not-in-list)

§§ TESTS
  put(A) put(B) put(C) : order [C, B, A]
  get(A) : order [A, C, B]
  cap=3 : put(D) evicts-B : order [D, A, C]
  get on-missing-key returns ∅

§§ ANTI
  N! linear-scan for-LRU ← requires doubly-linked-list
  N! unbounded-growth ← enforce cap-evict
  N! inconsistent-map-list ← unlink + remove always-paired

# @prose-file
# corpus-mode: pure-CSL
# tests: token-bucket rate limiter + burst allowance + refill schedule

§ rate-limiter.spec

§§ GOAL
  fn try-acquire (rl : &Limiter, cost : u32) -> bool
  W! limit rate ≤ configured-rps
  W! allow burst-up-to configured-burst
  W! fairness : FIFO when blocked-callers-queue

§§ DATA
  def Limiter'd = ⟨
    tokens      : f64,
    capacity    : f64,
    rate        : f64,       # tokens-per-second
    last-refill : timestamp,
  ⟩

§§ OPS

§§§ refill'f
  now = now'f
  elapsed = now - last-refill
  new-tokens = elapsed * rate
  tokens = min (capacity, tokens + new-tokens)
  last-refill = now

§§§ try-acquire'f
  refill ()
  cost ≤ tokens  →
    tokens = tokens - cost
    return true
  return false

§§§ wait-and-acquire'f
  refill ()
  cost > capacity  →  return false   # never-satisfiable
  while tokens < cost :
    needed = cost - tokens
    sleep-for (needed / rate)
    refill ()
  tokens = tokens - cost
  return true

§§ INVARIANTS
  W! 0 ≤ tokens ≤ capacity
  W! rate > 0
  W! refill-is-monotonic ← last-refill never-decreases
  N! tokens-negative (caller-skipped-refill)
  N! unbounded-wait without-configured-timeout
  N! concurrent-modification without-mutex

§§ STRATEGIES-COMPARED
  token-bucket  : allows-burst + simple-math + RECOMMENDED
  leaky-bucket  : smooths-output + no-burst
  fixed-window  : cheap + boundary-hot-spot
  sliding-window: accurate + O(log n) per-accept
  this-spec = token-bucket

§§ TESTS
  start-full + burst-of-capacity-requests : all-accepted
  exhausted + wait (1/rate) : one-more-accepted
  cost > capacity : always-rejected
  two-concurrent : total-accepted ≤ configured-capacity + t*rate

§§ ANTI
  N! clock-skew-correction-inside-refill ← caller-responsibility
  N! refill-per-request-even-when-not-needed ← batch-pattern prefer
  N! integer-tokens-when-cost-is-fractional
